standard.title: Algorithms and number patterns
standard.description: follow and create algorithms involving a sequence of steps and decisions to investigate numbers; describe any emerging patterns
standard.prior_knowledge: No direct predecessor in the progression map. Students have worked with number patterns informally through addition and multiplication, but have not yet explicitly followed or created step-by-step algorithms to generate or investigate number sequences.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students follow and create algorithms involving sequences of steps and decisions to investigate numbers, and describe any patterns that emerge.

nodes.label: Following an algorithm
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can follow a given step-by-step algorithm involving a sequence of operations and produce the correct numerical output.
nodes.minimum_width: Follow one provided algorithm (3–5 steps) applied to at least three different starting numbers; record each output.
nodes.typical_width: Follow several algorithms of varying complexity involving addition, subtraction and multiplication steps; record outputs systematically in a table.
wider: Follow algorithms that include decision points ('if the result is even, do X; if odd, do Y') and trace the different paths
Investigate the Collatz sequence or similar number algorithms as examples of algorithmic thinking applied to number investigation

response_modes.reason: Following an algorithm precisely requires students to track state across steps — a reasoning demand that benefits from explicit scaffolding of how to record intermediate results without losing place.

nodes.hinge_reason: Precise algorithm execution and systematic recording are prerequisite for Node 2 (creating algorithms) and Node 3 (describing patterns) — students who skip steps or fail to record outputs cannot produce the data needed to create or observe patterns. The skill of tracking state is the foundation the whole standard rests on.
success_criteria: Students can follow a step-by-step algorithm and produce correct outputs for given inputs.
Students can record their steps clearly showing how they reached the output.

nodes.label: Creating algorithms
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can create a simple algorithm (sequence of steps) to generate or investigate a number sequence.
nodes.minimum_width: Create an algorithm with at least three steps that, when applied to a starting number, generates a number sequence; test it with two starting values.
nodes.typical_width: Create algorithms to generate or transform number sequences; test and refine algorithms when outputs are unexpected; represent algorithms as numbered steps.
wider: Express algorithms as flowcharts with decision branches, extending beyond linear step sequences
Create algorithms to model real-world processes (e.g. a savings algorithm: 'start with $10, add $5 each week, stop when you reach $50')
success_criteria: Students can write a step-by-step algorithm that generates the intended output.
Students can test their algorithm with at least two starting values and check whether it produces the expected result.

nodes.label: Describing emerging patterns
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe a pattern they observe in the outputs of an algorithm, including whether it continues, repeats or terminates.
nodes.minimum_width: Apply an algorithm to generate at least six outputs and write one sentence describing a pattern they notice.
nodes.typical_width: Generate sequences from algorithms and describe patterns in terms of structure (growing, repeating, alternating); predict future values; explain why the pattern occurs.
wider: Connect algorithmic patterns to algebraic thinking — expressing patterns as rules (e.g. 'each term is 3 more than the previous')
Investigate whether changing one step of an algorithm changes the pattern — comparing two algorithms that differ by one step

response_modes.reason: Pattern description integrates algorithm following, output generation and mathematical observation. Students who can follow but not describe are missing the investigative dimension the descriptor requires.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Connecting patterns to rules and exploring algorithm variation provides genuine algebraic readiness — students begin to see patterns as generalisable rather than instance-specific, which is foundational for Y5–7 algebra.
success_criteria: Students can describe a pattern in the outputs of an algorithm using mathematical language (e.g. increasing by, repeating every).
Students can predict a future value in the sequence and justify the prediction based on the pattern.
